extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 including standards for reduction to practice, utility, reasonable diligence, effective filing dates, and form rejections. Primarily directed to examiner application of statutory bars and related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Device reduced to practice must include every limitation of the count
rubrics_metrics.description: The device reduced to practice must include every limitation of the count; every limitation in a count is material and must be proved to establish an actual reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Fredkin v. Irasek; Meitzner v. Corte; Hull v. Bonis. There is no doctrine of equivalents for establishing an actual reduction to practice — remedy is a preliminary motion to amend the count to conform to proofs. Examiner/advocate must show each claim limitation is present in the reduction-to-practice example or test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility must be known at time of reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is not actually reduced to practice unless there is a known (practical) utility at the time of reduction to practice (except for plant and design inventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Wiesner v. Weigert; Azar v. Burns; Ciric v. Flanigen; Engelhardt v. Judd; Rey-Bellet v. Engelhardt. For counts that do not recite a specific utility, evidence establishing a substantial utility for any purpose can suffice. Animal tests can be adequate in some circumstances where correlation to human utility exists or to show utility for animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable utility is generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A probable utility (highly likely or suggested by screening) does not establish practical utility for reduction to practice; practical utility is established by actual testing or when utility can be foretold with certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Bindra v. Kelly; Wu v. Jucker (screening tests insufficient). But consider Nelson v. Bowler: evidence judged as a whole and a reasonable correlation linking observed properties to suggested uses may suffice. Examiners must evaluate persuasiveness of the whole record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence standard does not require exclusive devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable diligence under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) relates to both 'attorney-diligence' and 'engineering-diligence' and does not require that an inventor or attorney drop all other work to focus solely on the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Keizer v. Bradley and Emery v. Ronden. Reasonable diligence is contextual — an attorney's reasonable backlog and chronological handling of cases can constitute diligence (Bey v. Kollonitsch). Examiners should consider both inventor and attorney activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical period for diligence (first conceiver but later reducer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical period for a first conceiver who is later to reduce to practice begins just prior to the entry in the field of the party who was first to reduce to practice and continues until the first conceiver reduces to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry into the field depends on what the first reducer relies on (e.g., conception plus reasonable diligence, actual reduction, or constructive reduction such as filing). Cite Hull v. Davenport; Fritsch v. Lin; Rebstock v. Flouret; Justus v. Appenzeller for examples and priority chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire diligence period must be accounted by acts or acceptable excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must account for the entire period during which diligence is required by either affirmative acts showing work toward reduction to practice or by acceptable excuses for inactivity; reasonably continuous diligence (not necessarily continuous) is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Perfect Surgical Techniques v. Olympus Am.; Gould v. Schawlow; In re Harry; In re Mulder; Fitzgerald v. Arbib. Small unexplained gaps (even 2 days) can be fatal in short critical periods. Evidence must be specific as to dates and facts (Kendall v. Searles). Many excuses (lack of funding, routine reporting, pursuing commercial exploitation) are insufficient; vacations/ill health may be considered depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh the body of evidence for reasonable continuous diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should weigh the collection of evidence over the entire critical period to determine whether the invention was not abandoned or unreasonably delayed; absence of daily or frequent records is not alone dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Perfect Surgical Techniques (841 F.3d). The point is to avoid scouring for gaps if the overall evidence shows lack of abandonment. In re Mulder does not mandate that any inactivity necessarily destroys a diligence claim — context and quantity of corroborating evidence matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work relied upon to show diligence must be directly related to the reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The work relied upon to show reasonable diligence must be directly related to the reduction to practice of the claimed invention; activity on related subject matter is insufficient unless it is closely related and directly advances reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Naber v. Cricchi; Scott v. Koyama; In re Jolley; Gunn v. Bosch; Ginos v. Nedelec. Preparatory acts (e.g., building plant to practice a process) can be credited; work on closely related inventions may be credited in some circumstances. Fortuitous reductions while working on a different invention do not show diligence toward the invention in issue. Corroboration requirements and specifics of the inventor's circumstances should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney diligence in preparing/filing application inures to inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence of an attorney preparing and filing the patent application inures to the benefit of the inventor; conception can be established by a draft finished by an attorney on behalf of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Haskell v. Coleburne; Bey v. Kollonitsch; Perfect Surgical Techniques. Short periods (e.g., six days) to execute and file can be acceptable. Reasonable diligence by the attorney (working reasonably hard during the continuous critical period) is sufficient; related work that contributes to preparation can be credited.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of diligence period marked by actual or constructive reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of the diligence period is marked by either an actual reduction to practice or a constructive reduction to practice (e.g., filing a patent application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Justus v. Appenzeller: it is of no moment that the end is fixed by constructive rather than actual reduction to practice. Examiners should treat constructive reduction (timely filed application) as closing the diligence period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102, the effective filing date of the claimed invention is the actual U.S. filing date of the application unless special situations apply (A, B, C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations: (A) continuation/divisional/priority under 35 U.S.C. 120/365(c) — effective date equals earliest in line if requirements met; (B) continuation-in-part — claims not supported by parent get new actual filing date; claims fully supported under 35 U.S.C. 112 get parent's effective date; (C) proper 35 U.S.C. 119(e) benefit to a provisional gives provisional filing date for fully supported claims. Note: national stage filing date and international filing date issues (MPEP cross-references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) first where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should first consider whether a reference qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (statutory bar) because a reference whose publication/issue date is more than one year prior to the effective filing date results in a statutory bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence of public use or sale activity >1 year pre-effective filing date exists, reject under 102(b) (statutory bar) rather than 102(a). Consider the one-year grace period and special rules when the grace period ends on a weekend/holiday (35 U.S.C. 21(b)). Be mindful of deposit/mail and electronic filing rules (37 CFR).

rubrics_metrics.name: When 102(b) does not apply consider pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the publication or issue date of the reference is too recent for 102(b) to apply, examiner should next consider whether pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) applies (applications/publications/patents as of certain filing dates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA 102(e) can give prior art effect as of certain U.S. filing dates, including certain international filing dates. For an international filing date to count for 102(e), the filing must be on or after Nov 29, 2000, designate the U.S., and be published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in English. The inventive entity of the application must be different from that of the reference — joint inventors partly in common may still permit application of 102(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) structure and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 102(e) has two clauses: (1) published patent applications (including certain international applications) and (2) U.S. patents. International filing dates on/after Nov 29, 2000 may serve as U.S. filing dates for 102(e) if conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References based on international applications filed prior to Nov 29, 2000 are subject to the 'pre-AIPA' version of 102(e) and have different prior art dates. Publications of international applications that do not meet the conditions may still be prior art under 102(a) or (b) as of their publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIPA (as of Nov 28, 2000) 102(e) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For international applications filed before Nov 29, 2000, the pre-AIPA version of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (as in force Nov 28, 2000) governs how those patents/applications may be used as prior art (dates tied to compliance with 371(c) or later U.S. continuing application filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents from international applications filed before Nov 29, 2000 may only be used as prior art based on compliance dates with 371(c)(1),(2),(4) or the filing date of a later-filed U.S. continuing application. Publications of such international applications do not have a pre-AIPA 102(e) date and are prior art under 102(a) or (b) as of their publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continue to consider pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) even if 102(e) applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a reference qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the examiner should still consider 102(a) for specific reasons (e.g., publication date under PCT Art 21(2) may be the earliest prior art date under 102(a); disqualification under 103(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102(a) applies when the publication date is earlier than the effective filing date and the reference is not the inventor's own work. If the evidence points to knowledge within the year prior to filing, apply 102(a) rather than 102(b). Also consider common ownership / obligation of assignment that may disqualify a 102(e) reference under 103(c) when used in an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Office actions should use standardized form paragraphs for rejections under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (e.g., ¶7.06, ¶7.07.fti, ¶7.08.fti, ¶7.09.fti, ¶7.10.fti, ¶7.11.fti, ¶7.12.fti), with specific ordering and usage rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶7.06 must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013 that claims priority to an application filed before March 16, 2013; use it only once per Office action. ¶7.07.fti quotes the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 statutory text and is required in first actions on the merits and final rejections (and used only once per action). Other ¶7.0x.fti paragraphs correspond to specific 102(a)-(e) grounds and must be preceded by ¶7.07.fti as indicated. Examiner notes in the MPEP explain precise sequencing and when each paragraph should or must be used.
